before: "Bread" and "the one coming down" is the nourishing word of God, which the one coming to Him eats by making virtue active. Or, those partaking in His teaching by practicing virtue are said to eat, but by the intellectual examination of the hidden meaning of Scripture, they are said to drink, just as Christ says: "Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness" (Matt 5:6), those partaking in this by both practice and thought.

The Jews present, having misunderstood the Savior's saying that the one keeping the word will not see death (John 8:51), supposed that to taste it meant the same as seeing death; for it seemed to them that based on His words, He would not taste death without having experienced the cosmic death; but this seems to overturn the Lord's promise, since those who kept His word have died, and their desire has become a deceitful trickery through a false similarity. For the one keeping the word of Jesus will not see the death that follows sin (John 8:52), even if he shall taste the common and bodily death. Since the prophets also said "they died" without adding "all," Enoch and Elijah do not fight against the not having died.
What does He mean by "day"—the intellectual day of the Lord (John 8:56)?

The "eyes of the heart" have been enlightened (John 9:37), shining by the light of the true one. The one opposite, being blinded by that which causes ignorance, seems not to have sin because he does not act willingly or sluggishly sinning. But this ignorance in another way is sin; for it was logical to have the knowledge of good and evil. Therefore, he is accused for the neglect of this, in favor of that ignorance. For this, the "slave who did not know the will of the master will be given little" (Luke 12:47).
The word of God becomes a door to those entering toward God according to "enter before Him in gladness" (Ps 100:2); with this, the mind is inside the man, but the body is outside.

Saying that one, attending to the inner man, enters through the Word which is a door, just as the dead, surrounding 'the members upon the earth' and 'the death of Jesus in the flesh' around himself, goes out 'through the door' striving to be pleasing even to one not residing within. 16 John 10:29 The Father gives to the Son those having been made according to the good as having an unsurpassed quality; for 'all that the Father gives to me shall come to me', and 'behold, I and the children whom God has given to me'. For just as the Son leads to the Father and hands over to him those to whom he touches himself to provide for understanding according to the one who 'having seen me has seen the Father', so the Father gives these to the Son, whom he makes known to them, just as to Peter; for not 'flesh and blood, but the Father has revealed' the Son. All those having known the Son thus from the Father attain to those things given to the Son through the exceeding perfection of these having such things. How [about] Judas? Being one of those given by the Father to the Son according to the ones 'whom I have given', and 'no one was lost of them except the son of perdition', he fell from such great magnitude as to be called 'a son of perdition'; for there was not yet room in the construction for Judas to be evil, as the heterodox suppose, such a change being found concerning him.

before: Providing more or less than this; for being and essence and knowledge are not naturally comparable by a simple measure or quantity of magnitude. Why then was it said? The Savior, in a single word, extended a twofold manner of teaching; for the meaning of the spoken verb is double. For example, through 'he who sent me,' he pointed to a body contained in places, capable of being described, and not to his indescribable divinity encompassing all things. But through the comparative verb 'to say,' he shows his divinity to be greater when compared to the Father, since he is of the same essence, yet in the assumption of the body, being thought of the Father as lesser according to his becoming man. And do not marvel if the Savior, having become man, says he is lesser than the Father, when it is also said of the angels that they are shorter: 'We see Jesus, being made a little inferior to the angels (Hebrews 2:7), through the suffering of death, being crowned with glory and honor.' And it was also said of his own disciples that they are lesser: 'I am among you as one who serves (Luke 22:27),' and as the least. Therefore, the things being compared are of the same essence, but the simple things, both in knowledge and in essence, do not admit of the greater and the lesser. But if, regarding the divinity of the Son and without having taken flesh, you wish to take 'he who sent me' to mean the Father is greater than me, you will give him as being contained and enclosed in places, being sent to where he was not, and being moved from where he is; which is absurd.

The Father glorified his own Son, placing him under the sun with his scepters, and he himself was also counter-glorified through this; for the Son was glorified by the Father, having been believed by all, that he is the offspring and fruit of the One who is strong in all things. And the Father was counter-glorified as if by his own offspring; for since the offspring was easily known to be able to accomplish all things, the grace of the glory passed over to the one who begot him. Just as, he says, you glorified and were counter-glorified, having given to him the authority and lordship over all according to what was clearly said.

In what way, I wish, so that nothing of what has been given is lost; for glory itself passes into us. For it was necessary that the transcendent, having become entirely under hand, be saved once for all by the all-powerful God the Word and remain in the good things eternally, so as to be no longer tyrannized by death, nor held by corruption or by sins, nor be subject to the ancient evils.

This is what he says: 'Reveal to those who do not know, manifest to me the glory which I have from God the Word' (Jo 17:1–3). For 'no one' 'is able' to 'come to me, unless the Father who sent me draws him' (Jo 6:44). Likewise, it is to hear also the Son glorifying the Father by revealing him to those who do not know God. In this same way, the Holy Spirit is said to glorify the Son by revealing him to those who are ignorant. And even if here—concerning him—it is to be imagined forever. This is the eternal—they cast out the Son of God. But it is necessary to know this: that the cause is instead of the caused; for knowing the truth brings us eternal life.

The pre-cosmic glory of the Son of God would be something other than God the Word himself, that 'true light' (Jo 1:9); for he is not glorified by another glory through another, being other than the glory, but as previously said, he is the 'Lord of glory' and King of glory. But since 'he emptied himself, having taken the form of a slave' (Phil 2:7)—for the 'Word,' he says, 'became flesh' (Jo 1:14) and we saw him 'and he had neither form nor beauty' (Isa 53:2)—and many disbelieved in such a descent, many disbelieved that God became man for this purpose, desiring to reveal his divinity to those who do not know, he says: 'Father, glorify your Son' (Jo 17:1), which is to say: reveal to those who do not know, manifest to me the glory which I have from God the Word. Therefore Paul said, 'when it pleased' God 'to reveal his Son in me, that I might preach him among the Gentiles' (Gal 1:16).
